video_title: Inside the Team That Killed Mandatory Code Review — Quinn Slack, AMP
gist: Quinn Slack, CEO of AMP (the 20-person coding-agent company spun out of Sourcegraph), describes a working model in which mandatory pre-merge code review, local dev environments, and eventually CI have all been eliminated in favor of cloud-run agents ('orbs') operating in parallel with scoped, short-lived production credentials. He argues the resulting stack displaces GitHub, off-the-shelf SaaS dashboards, and most non-engineering headcount, while the host (swyx) counters on where deterministic CI and human labor still hold.

insights.claim: AMP has had no mandatory code review before merging to main since the product's inception, treating review as a bottleneck rather than a quality gate.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: If trust-plus-agents replaces review at more teams, the PR-review workflow layer (GitHub PRs, review-automation startups, AI code-review vendors) loses its structural position in the dev pipeline.
insights.quote: Mandatory code review before it gets to Maine. Yeah, it's dead. It's been dead ever since we started working on AMP.

insights.claim: The prerequisite for removing code review is not tooling but a small, fully accountable team with end-to-end ownership and equity-level skin in the game, which AI makes affordable because you no longer hire people you don't trust to do low-agency work.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: Signals a hiring-model shift: fewer, more senior, more trusted hires per unit of output, which compresses seat-based tooling TAM and headcount growth at AI-native software companies.
insights.quote: you do not have the need to go and hire people that you do not trust that you do not trust have high agency or the right skills because you can use an agent to do those things

insights.claim: For fast-moving end-user software, optimizing for mean time to recovery (shipping a fix within 15 minutes of a log or customer signal) beats optimizing for mean time between failures, and produces higher quality than waiting days for review.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: A reusable diligence lens: ask whether a portfolio company's release process is MTTR- or MTBF-shaped, since the former is what unlocks agent-driven parallel shipping.

insights.claim: Mandatory review is what blocks companies from benefiting from agent parallelism, because stacking 20 agent-generated changes behind a human review queue produces no throughput gain.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: Explains why remote-agent adoption stalls in review-gated enterprises; vendors selling parallel agents must sell a process change, not just a product.
insights.quote: my company if we have to review code then what's the benefit of me stacking up 20 things that are waiting for review you know I don't benefit from greater parallelism

themes.theme: Local dev is dead, orbs win

insights.claim: AMP's remote-execution product ('orbs') drove more change in how the team and its customers build software in three to four weeks than the entirety of the prior year of AI coding adoption.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: A concrete adoption-velocity datapoint for the shift from local CLI agents to cloud agent runtimes — the segment to watch for share moves over the next two quarters.
insights.quote: our customers are using orbs more in the last three or four weeks than all of the change to how we build software that happened last year. And last year was not some quiet year.

insights.claim: Once remote agent environments make dev servers, previews and parallel workspaces 'just work', developers abandon local development voluntarily rather than by security mandate — the guest had not run his local dev server in two weeks.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: Value migrates from laptop-resident IDE/CLI tools to hosted dev-environment infrastructure; watch spend shifting to sandbox and remote-env providers.
insights.quote: So you know local dev in our opinion is dead and that's been a huge change

insights.claim: Cloud agents with scoped, short-lived credentials (e.g. an OIDC token granting 30 minutes of read-only access to production logs or the database) are more secure than the status quo of a coding agent on a developer laptop inheriting every credential that developer has authorized.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: Security teams flipping from blocker to buyer is the accelerant for cloud agent adoption; creates a market for agent identity, scoped-credential and audit tooling.
insights.quote: we've heard from some of our customers using AMP that they, you know, had this other script that happened to be authenticated and it found a way to like a production console

insights.claim: Because both developer experience and security improve simultaneously, the transition away from locally run CLI coding agents could be essentially complete within roughly two months.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: An aggressive, falsifiable near-term call: if right, local-first coding agent products face rapid obsolescence; if wrong, it marks vendor overreach.
insights.quote: I don't know, in 2 months, we could be seeing CLI coding agents is basically dead.

insights.claim: Agents can now run staged production database migrations autonomously — deploying a phase, monitoring logs and database invariants, then advancing or rolling back — replacing work that previously occupied a developer and several ops people babysitting a rollout.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: Agent value is expanding from code authoring into ops/release engineering, putting incident-response and deployment-tooling vendors into the blast radius.
insights.quote: I had it push out a few stages that were pretty safe and monitor the logs. And if everything was good, then it would go on to the next phase. And if not, then it would roll back.

insights.claim: The differentiator among remote agent products is not the capability itself but driving setup friction to near zero, since the same idea was pioneered years earlier by Devin and is now being copied across the category.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: Category is converging fast on the same architecture, so competitive moats come from execution on environment reliability rather than novel positioning.

insights.claim: AMP deliberately deleted features — including its editor extension — earning a reputation for removing more than it added, on the theory that keeping users on the old way of working is negative value in a fast-moving AI market.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: Inverts the usual SaaS retention playbook; product-velocity-over-compatibility is becoming a screening signal for which AI tool vendors survive.
insights.quote: with AI moving so fast, the value of keeping users on doing the old thing is is actually negative

insights.claim: The technology adoption cycle has compressed from 5-10 years of user lock-in to roughly three months, after which a vendor that has not pulled its users to the frontier is perceived as obsolete.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: If true, revenue durability assumptions and LTV models for AI dev-tool companies need drastically shorter half-lives.
insights.quote: in the past, you would have a 5 or 10 year technology cycle and you could acquire a user and then they'd be with you for 10 years. But now, if you're not nudging them, yanking them to be on the frontier with you, then 3 months later, they're going to say, "Hey, who are these fools in their product? It's obsolete."

themes.theme: GitHub, CI and the sandbox layer

insights.claim: AMP has effectively stopped using GitHub — no issues, no pull requests, barely any Actions — keeping it only to push the repo while moving to AMP-hosted and Pierre-hosted repositories.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: The first credible defection pattern away from GitHub as the default developer surface; watch code-hosting startups and agent vendors bundling repo storage.
insights.quote: it's not like AMP is the GitHub killer. It's the next GitHub. These things don't die with a bang. They die with a a whimper.

insights.claim: Roughly half the AMP team argues CI is unnecessary because the agent already runs tests in a reproducible team-standard sandbox, leaving only image packaging and deployment as genuinely required pipeline steps.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: Directly threatens the CI/CD vendor category; the counter-argument (deterministic exhaustive test runs, undetected cross-module breakage) is the thing to test in diligence.
insights.quote: the days of of CI as we know it are numbered

insights.claim: The host's defense of CI is that agents only run what is in their context and cannot be trusted to be exhaustive on a large codebase, making CI valuable specifically as a deterministic full-coverage stage feeding failures back to the agent.
insights.speaker: host (swyx)
insights.so_what: Frames the surviving niche for CI vendors: deterministic exhaustive verification and flake elimination, not orchestration.
insights.quote: you don't trust the agent to be exhaustive. like it'll run what's in its context, but if you have a large project, you don't know that it's run everything that it should run

insights.claim: Even as classic CI declines, the underlying demand for reproducible ephemeral environments is exploding, with some users running a hundred orbs per day and sandbox providers like E2B and Daytona growing rapidly.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: The compute-substrate layer beneath agents is the clearer growth trade than the agent UI layer; sandbox infra is a picks-and-shovels position.
insights.quote: there's people that have a hundred orbs per day and you know, companies like E2B and Daytona and all these sandbox companies are absolutely blowing up

insights.claim: AMP runs on E2B and finds that large cloud providers shipping 'sandbox' products lack basic primitives such as resume or network access, while AMP receives three or four cold pitches a week from competing sandbox startups.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: Startup-vs-hyperscaler gap in sandbox primitives is real today but the space is crowding fast; margin pressure is coming as AMP pushes for lower per-orb cost.
insights.quote: they like lack the ability to resume or like their sandboxes have no network access or something like that. And it's just it's bizarre.

themes.theme: Agents as the settings screen: jellyware

insights.claim: An agent plus code is the ultimate settings screen, so companies can spin up ad hoc internal software — such as a custom dashboard replacing a Looker query and an MCP integration — instead of buying configurable off-the-shelf tools.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: Direct bear case for horizontal internal-tooling SaaS (BI, dashboards, admin tools) where configurability was the product.
insights.quote: why even have that at a certain You have ultimate customizability. You don't need a setting screen. You don't need a complex integration and MCP and all of the overhead that's entailed by buying some off-the-shelf software package

insights.claim: The decisive asymmetry in software economics is that self-hosted single-user software is far easier to make robust, while multi-tenancy and settings roughly double complexity — so users can now build better-fitting tools than any third-party vendor could sell them.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: The clearest articulated mechanism for AI-driven SaaS disintermediation; use it to grade which SaaS categories are exposed (single-tenant, low-guarantee) versus defended (multi-tenant guarantees, compliance).
insights.quote: It's so much easier for you to build something that's going to be self-hosted that just has to solve one person's problem and to make that really robust. But if you're trying to build multi-tenency, I mean that doubles the complexity.

insights.claim: Coding SaaS will be the last SaaS standing because every other SaaS becomes buildable through it.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: The maximalist version of the disintermediation thesis, and the implicit investment case for concentrating dev-tool exposure rather than broad SaaS exposure.
insights.quote: coding SAS will be the last SAS in the world because all the other SAS will just be buildable via coding SAS

insights.claim: AMP plans to release its internal tools as 'jellyware' — code others can remix and customize with their own agent — replacing both the open-source maintenance burden and the traditional path of adding settings, integrations and a sales motion.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: A new distribution primitive between open source and product; watch whether remixable agent-customizable code erodes the small-tool SaaS long tail.
insights.quote: It's like softer than software but it's not totally vibe coded and you can customize it with your own agent.

insights.claim: Publishing agent skills — markdown plus sample code that ports to any project — is becoming more valuable than publishing a library, and is now the host's main use of GitHub.
insights.speaker: host (swyx)
insights.so_what: Distribution and mindshare in AI dev tooling may accrue to skill/prompt repositories rather than package registries — a new place to watch for ecosystem lock-in.
insights.quote: that is probably the new open source, which is you open source some markdown files with some sample code

insights.claim: Sourcegraph spun AMP out as a separate 20-person company with investors and employees holding shares in both entities — a structure the guest says has barely been attempted since David Sacks spun Yammer out of Geni around 2009.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: A replicable template for incumbents whose AI product outgrows the legacy business; compare against the Intercom/Fin in-house path when evaluating similar forks.
insights.quote: we decided to spin off which has not been done really in like startups and software since David Saxs spun off Yammer from Genie in like 2009

insights.claim: Sourcegraph's code search counts nine of the ten largest public tech companies, four of the six largest banks, Uber and Stripe as customers — the enterprise base the guest built before choosing to run a 20-person team instead.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: Establishes that the anti-scale argument here comes from someone who successfully sold to the largest enterprises, raising the signal value of the pivot.
insights.quote: We have like nine of the 10 top public tech companies as customers and like four of the six top banks and like Uber and Stripe

insights.claim: Companies at roughly 20 people that respond by hiring a PM or a marketer are following the obsolete playbook that ends with 10% of staff building the product and 90% managing the overhead of selling it.
insights.speaker: Quinn Slack
insights.so_what: If AI-native companies hold headcount flat while scaling revenue, per-seat GTM software and recruiting demand shrink even as software output rises.
insights.quote: ultimately that's going to lead to something where 10% of the people are thinking about how to make a great product and the other 90% are thinking about the overhead that you know how to how to sell it

insights.claim: The host has used Codex as a de facto CMO for two months running ads and advising on SEO and AEO, judging the results roughly equal to a human consultant and the experience preferable.
insights.speaker: host (swyx)
insights.so_what: A first-hand substitution datapoint for the fractional-CMO and marketing-consulting market, the kind of services spend most exposed to general agents.
insights.quote: Codeex has been my CMO for the last like 2 months, basically running our ads and giving me advice on AEO and SEO and what have you.

insights.claim: Human video editing remains cheap and good enough that AI clipping tools are not worth adopting for a high-production media business, and an A16Z-backed clipping product tested poorly.
insights.speaker: host (swyx)
insights.so_what: A rare stated non-adoption case: AI video tooling faces a quality bar it has not cleared for premium producers, so growth likely comes from low-budget long-tail buyers.
insights.quote: Everyone else is looking for a good person to do that. So I think you are the apex predator of this.

insights.claim: Jeff Dean's departure from Google to work with about five people is read as an implicit critique of thousand-person AI org structures and as evidence that the small-elite-team model is spreading to the most senior researchers.
insights.speaker: host (swyx)
insights.so_what: Talent flight from large AI orgs to five-person teams is a leading indicator for where frontier output and future funding rounds land.
insights.quote: his mission statement when he left Google was like, what could a small handful of people do as opposed to like thousands of people?
